scenarios.title: Planning Your Study Path
scenarios.situation: You have 3 weeks before your DevSecOps Mastery interview/exam. You've just opened this bootcamp with 15 domains ahead of you.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most effective study sequence?
choices: Start Here lessons → core domains in order → Systems Anatomy → Mock Assessment → Capstone, doing drills daily
Jump straight to the Mock Assessment to see where you stand
Study only your weakest domain until it's perfect, then move on
Read all lessons first, then do all scenarios, then all labs
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The bootcamp is sequenced deliberately: orientation first, then progressive domain mastery with interleaved drills for retention, Systems Anatomy to connect it all, mock under realistic conditions, capstone to prove it. Jumping to the mock wastes its diagnostic value; perfecting one domain starves the others; batching by activity type kills interleaving benefits.
scenarios.hint: What does each phase prepare you for? What happens if you skip the foundation?

scenarios.title: The Passive Reader Trap
scenarios.situation: A learner has 'completed' 40 lessons but fails every scenario. They read each lesson carefully and passed all knowledge checks on the first try.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what's the fix?
choices: They consumed passively without application — the fix is interleaving scenarios immediately after lessons and doing teach-backs aloud
The lessons are too easy — skip to harder material
They need to re-read the lessons more carefully
Knowledge checks are broken — report a bug
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Passing knowledge checks proves recognition, not application. Scenarios demand transfer — using knowledge in novel situations. The fix is structural: never finish a lesson without immediately attempting its scenarios, and explain each concept aloud (teach-back) to expose shallow understanding.
scenarios.hint: What's the difference between recognizing an answer and producing one under pressure?

scenarios.title: Where does the SAST scan go?
scenarios.situation: Your team just bought a SAST tool. The security team wants it to run as a nightly batch over the whole codebase; developers worry findings will pile up unread.
scenarios.prompt: Where in the pipeline should SAST run for maximum effect?
evidence: dev push -> CI (build, unit test) -> nightly security batch -> deploy Friday
choices: Run SAST on every pull request as a required check, scoped to changed code with a baseline — developers get fast, relevant feedback where they can still fix it cheaply.
Keep it nightly over the whole codebase — broader coverage finds more issues.
Run SAST only right before production deploys as a final gate.
Run SAST manually once a quarter during security reviews.
scenarios.why: Security feedback follows the same economics as test feedback: cheapest at the point of authorship. PR-scoped SAST with baselining gives developers actionable findings on their own diff; nightly whole-codebase scans produce unactionable backlogs, and pre-deploy gates arrive when fixes are most expensive.
scenarios.hint: When is a vulnerability cheapest to fix — while the author still has the code open, or weeks later from a backlog?

scenarios.title: The vulnerable base image
scenarios.situation: Your container image is built FROM a popular public base image. A scan reports 40 critical CVEs — all in the base image's OS packages, none in your application code. Rebuilding from scratch would take weeks.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best remediation?
evidence:
trivy image myapp:1.2
Total: 40 (CRITICAL: 40, all in debian base packages)
FROM debian:bookworm in Dockerfile
choices: Switch to a minimal base image (distroless or minimal) and pin the digest; add package updates in the build so the image carries only what the app needs.
Add a comment in the Dockerfile noting the CVEs are not in your code.
Suppress the 40 findings in the scanner so the pipeline goes green.
Stop scanning images — the CVEs are in the OS layer, not your responsibility.
scenarios.why: Most base-image CVEs come from packages your app never uses — a minimal or distroless base removes the attack surface instead of patching it. Pinning the digest makes builds reproducible. Suppressing findings or ignoring the OS layer leaves exploitable code in your shipped artifact.
scenarios.hint: The vulnerabilities live in packages your app doesn't need. What's the smallest base that still runs your app?

scenarios.title: DAST found it, SAST didn't
scenarios.situation: A DAST scan against staging found an authentication bypass. SAST never flagged it — the flaw is in how two services interact at runtime, invisible in static analysis of either repo alone.
scenarios.prompt: What does this teach about scan strategy?
evidence:
DAST: POST /api/admin/users without token returns 200 (staging)
SAST: 0 findings on both services
choices: SAST and DAST are complementary: SAST finds code-level flaws early, DAST finds runtime/interaction flaws — run both, since neither covers the other's blind spots.
Replace SAST with DAST since DAST found the real bug.
The SAST tool is broken — file a vendor ticket and wait.
Disable the admin endpoint instead of fixing the scan gap.
scenarios.why: SAST analyzes code without running it (great for injection, hardcoded secrets) while DAST tests the running app (great for auth flows, session handling, service interactions). The bypass lived in runtime behavior across services — structurally invisible to SAST. Defense in depth means layering both, plus SCA for dependencies.
scenarios.hint: One tool reads code, the other attacks a running system. Could any single perspective catch both classes of flaw?

scenarios.title: The pipeline needs a policy
scenarios.situation: Security wants guarantees: no image with a critical CVE reaches production, and every deploy to prod needs a signed attestation. Today these are wiki pages everyone ignores.
scenarios.prompt: How do you enforce this as code?
evidence:
"Policy: no critical CVEs in prod. All prod deploys must be signed."
# compliance: 12% (measured by audit sample)
choices: Implement policy as code (e.g. OPA/Conftest gates in CI, admission controllers in-cluster): the scan results and signatures become machine-checked inputs, and violating artifacts are blocked automatically.
Make the wiki page required reading during onboarding.
Have a security engineer manually approve every production deploy.
Add the policy text as comments in the deployment YAML.
scenarios.why: Policy as code turns unenforceable prose into deterministic gates: the pipeline evaluates scan results and signature attestations and refuses to promote non-compliant artifacts. Manual approvals don't scale and get rubber-stamped; comments and wiki pages have no enforcement mechanism.
scenarios.hint: The policy exists but compliance is 12%. What would make a violating deploy technically impossible instead of merely discouraged?

scenarios.title: Whose vulnerability is it anyway?
scenarios.situation: A critical CVE is announced in a transitive dependency — a library of a library, four levels deep. Your SCA tool flags it, but the vulnerable code path isn't reachable from your application. Upgrading breaks the build.
scenarios.prompt: How should you triage this?
evidence:
npm audit / grype report
CRITICAL CVE-2026-XXXX in dep-of-dep-of-dep
Reachability analysis: vulnerable function never called by app code
choices: Use reachability/VEX analysis to deprioritize the non-exploitable finding, document the assessment, schedule the upgrade normally — and fix the build breakage as tech debt rather than under incident pressure.
Drop everything and upgrade immediately regardless of the broken build — critical means critical.
Suppress the CVE permanently since it's not reachable.
Remove the SCA scanner — unreachable findings are noise.
scenarios.why: Not all critical CVEs are exploitable in your context — reachability analysis (and VEX statements) distinguish theoretical from actual risk. Treating every transitive critical as a fire drill burns out teams; permanent suppression without documentation hides risk. The disciplined path: assess, document, schedule the upgrade, fix the underlying build fragility.
scenarios.hint: Severity scores describe the vulnerability in isolation. What additional fact determines whether it threatens you?

scenarios.title: Signing the supply chain
scenarios.situation: After a dependency-confusion incident at a peer company, your CTO asks: how do we prove that the artifact in production is exactly what our pipeline built from the reviewed commit?
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct supply-chain integrity design?
evidence: Peer company shipped a poisoned package: registry served attacker code under a trusted name
choices: Sign artifacts at build time (Sigstore/cosign), generate SLSA-style provenance attestations linking artifact to source commit and build, and verify signatures + attestations at deploy time with policy enforcement.
Only pull dependencies from the public registry's 'verified' badge publishers.
Checksum the final image and email the checksum to the team for manual comparison.
Trust the CI system — it has authentication, so its outputs are trustworthy.
scenarios.why: Signing plus provenance closes the loop: the signature proves who built it, the attestation proves what source and build produced it, and deploy-time verification makes tampering fail closed. Publisher badges and CI auth are trust assumptions, not verification; emailed checksums are unscalable theater.
scenarios.hint: You need a chain of evidence from reviewed commit to running artifact that a machine can verify. What two artifacts provide that?

scenarios.title: The DevSecOps Mastery Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that DevSecOps Mastery is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in DevSecOps Mastery?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — DevSecOps Mastery issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — DevSecOps Mastery is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is DevSecOps Mastery supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any DevSecOps Mastery failure in Devsecops Mastery.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to DevSecOps Mastery
evidence: All DevSecOps Mastery components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

lessons.title: DevSecOps — Core concepts
concepts: Shift-left means security feedback at authorship time: SAST on pull requests, secret scanning pre-commit (enforced in CI), and image scans on every build — findings are cheapest where the code is still open.
SAST, DAST, and SCA see different things: static code flaws, runtime behavior, and dependency vulnerabilities — layer all three because each has blind spots the others cover.
Containers shrink the attack surface: minimal/distroless bases, pinned digests, non-root users, and scanned layers turn the image into a deliberate artifact instead of an accident.
Policy as code (OPA/Conftest, admission controllers) makes security requirements machine-enforced gates rather than wiki prose — non-compliant artifacts physically cannot promote.
Supply-chain integrity is signatures plus provenance: sign what you build, attest where it came from (SLSA), and verify at deploy time so tampering fails closed.
Triage with reachability: not every critical CVE is exploitable in your app — assess exploitability, document with VEX, and schedule upgrades sanely instead of firefighting every scanner alert.

example.code:
# CI security stage (conceptual)
- name: Scan image
  run: |
    trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 myapp:${{ github.sha }}
- name: Policy check
  run: conftest test --policy policy/ deployment.yaml
example.walkthrough: Trivy fails the build on high/critical CVEs in the image, and Conftest evaluates the deployment manifest against OPA policies (e.g. 'must run as non-root'). Both run before any push to a registry or deploy — violating artifacts never leave CI.

pitfalls: Common trap: nightly whole-codebase SAST producing unactionable backlogs — scope scans to the PR diff with baselines.
Common trap: base64 'encrypted' secrets and suppressed scanner findings — both hide risk instead of reducing it.
Common trap: treating every scanner critical as an incident — use reachability/VEX triage or the team burns out.
Common trap: signing without verification — a signature nobody checks at deploy time is decoration.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Devsecops Mastery move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

TRIGGER event occurs

  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in

Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: Capstone: Secure Pipeline Project — Project Brief
concepts: Your capstone: a CI/CD pipeline with security gates at every stage and a threat-modeled app
Why a capstone matters: interviewers remember stories about things you built far longer than quiz scores. This is your proof.
Build in public: commit early, commit often. A git history showing iterative progress impresses more than a perfect final upload.
Document as you go: every decision gets a one-line reason in the README. Future-you (and interviewers) will thank present-you.

lessons.title: Capstone: Secure Pipeline Project — Build Guide
concepts: Milestone 1 — Foundation: scaffold the project, verify the toolchain works end-to-end before adding complexity.
Milestone 2 — Core: implement the central functionality. This is the demoable heart of the project.
Milestone 3 — Hardening: handle errors, add validation, make it robust enough to demo without fear.
Milestone 4 — Polish: README, diagrams, clean output. This is what separates 'homework' from 'portfolio'.
Testing each milestone: define 'done' as a verifiable behavior, not a feeling. Write the check before the code.
Narrative prep: for each milestone, prepare a 60-second explanation — what it does, why it matters, what was hard.

example.code:
Definition of done (example, Milestone 2):

  ✓ Core feature works with valid input
  ✓ Graceful error on invalid input
  ✓ Output verified against expected result
  ✓ Committed with a clear message
  ✓ README section updated

No milestone is done until all boxes check.

pitfalls: Skipping the hardening milestone — demos fail live, and robustness is what interviewers probe.
No verifiable 'done' criteria — 'it works on my machine' is not done.
Building all milestones before testing any — integrate and verify incrementally.

lessons.title: Capstone: Secure Pipeline Project — Demo & Interview Prep
concepts: The 5-minute demo arc: problem (30s) → approach (60s) → live walkthrough (2.5min) → lessons learned (60s).
Anticipate the deep questions: 'Why did you choose X over Y?' 'What breaks at scale?' 'What would you do differently?'
Resume bullet formula: Action verb + what you built + tech + measurable outcome. Quantify everything you can.
LinkedIn/portfolio: screenshots or a 60-second screen recording outperform text descriptions 10:1.
Bring the repo to interviews: offer to walk through the code. Few candidates do this — it signals genuine ownership.
Post-mortem: write 5 lines on what you'd improve. Interviewers love candidates who can critique their own work.

simulations.title: The scanner cried wolf
simulations.brief: The SCA scan flags 14 critical CVEs in the payment service on a Friday afternoon. The team wants to freeze the release. Triage before anyone panics.

steps.symptom: 14 critical CVEs flagged in dependencies of the payment service. Release freeze proposed.
evidence: 14 critical, 31 high. All in transitive dependencies.
Vulnerable package libfoo 2.1: used by the PDF export feature only. Payment path: no.
options: Triage with reachability: confirm which CVEs touch the payment path before freezing anything
Freeze the release immediately — 14 criticals is 14 criticals
Suppress all 14 — scanners always overreact
Upgrade every dependency tonight
steps.explain: Not every critical CVE is exploitable in your app. Reachability analysis — does the vulnerable code path execute in your deployment? — separates the real fires from scanner noise. Triage first, then act proportionally.

steps.symptom: 2 of the 14 are reachable in the payment path. The other 12 are not.
evidence: Reachable: CVE-A (auth lib), CVE-B (TLS lib). Unreachable: 12 others (PDF export, dev tooling, test fixtures).
VEX statements drafted for the 12 unreachable: status 'not_affected', justification 'vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path'.
options: Fix the 2 reachable now; document the 12 with VEX and schedule their upgrades sanely
Fix all 14 tonight regardless of reachability
Fix the 2 and delete the VEX drafts — documentation is overhead
Only fix CVE-A — one at a time
steps.explain: Reachability triage done right: the 2 reachable get immediate fixes, the 12 unreachable get VEX 'not_affected' statements with justification plus scheduled upgrades. Firefighting every scanner alert equally is how teams burn out and miss the real ones.

steps.symptom: Next sprint, the same 12 CVEs get flagged again and a new engineer panics.
evidence: Same 12 CVEs re-flagged. New engineer: 'Are we ignoring criticals?!'
No documented triage policy. VEX drafts were never published to the artifact metadata.
options: Publish the VEX statements with the artifacts and write the triage policy down so the next engineer inherits the reasoning
Tell the engineer to calm down — experience will teach them
Re-triage from scratch every sprint
Disable the scanner for that service
steps.explain: Triage that lives in one person's head isn't triage — it's folklore. VEX statements travel with the artifact, and a written policy means the next engineer sees 'not_affected with justification and a scheduled upgrade' instead of a mystery.

simulations.debrief: Triage with reachability: assess exploitability, document with VEX, fix what's reachable now, schedule the rest. Scanner output is raw signal — triage is what turns it into security work.

simulations.title: Secret in the repo
simulations.brief: A production database password was committed to the repo 6 months ago and just discovered during an audit. The commit is in history, forks exist, and the password is still valid. Work the response.

steps.symptom: Audit finds a live production DB password in git history, committed 6 months ago.
evidence: config/prod.env with DB_PASSWORD=... committed 2026-04-02. Still valid today. Forks: 11.
Proposal: 'Delete the file in a new commit.'
options: Rotate the credential immediately — history can't be un-pushed, so the secret is burned the moment it's discovered
Delete the file in a new commit and move on
Rewrite git history to remove it — that un-exposes it
It's been 6 months with no incident — leave it
steps.explain: A committed secret is a burned secret: forks, clones, and backups preserve it forever, and history rewrites don't reach them. Step one is always rotate the credential — containment before cleanup.

steps.symptom: Credential rotated. Now prevent the next one.
evidence: No secret scanning in pre-commit or CI. Developers commit .env files 'temporarily' regularly.
Pipeline: build, test, deploy. No scan stages.
options: Enforce secret scanning pre-commit and as a blocking CI stage — findings are cheapest where the code is still open
Send a reminder email about not committing secrets
Ban .env files entirely — developers will figure it out
Scan quarterly — continuous scanning slows developers down
steps.explain: Shift-left means feedback at authorship time: pre-commit hooks catch the secret before it exists in history, and a blocking CI scan catches what hooks miss. A reminder email is not a control; an enforced gate is.

steps.symptom: The app still needs the database password at runtime — it has to live somewhere.
evidence: App reads DB_PASSWORD from environment. Currently: committed .env file.
Candidates: secrets manager with runtime injection, encrypted file in repo, shared team vault copy-paste.
options: Move it to a secrets manager with runtime injection — the app gets the value at deploy time, never from the repo
Keep the .env but gitignore it — developers manage their own copies
Encrypt the .env and commit the key next to it for convenience
Paste it into the team chat when deploying
steps.explain: Secrets belong in a secrets manager resolved at runtime, not in the repo in any form. Gitignored local copies drift, committed keys defeat the encryption, and chat is a broadcast. The manager is the single source with audit and rotation.

simulations.debrief: Committed secrets are burned secrets: rotate first, then enforce pre-commit and CI scanning, then move runtime secrets to a manager. Each layer addresses a different stage of the secret's life.

simulations.title: The unsigned artifact that shipped
simulations.brief: An incident review finds last month's production deploy ran an image nobody can trace to a CI build. No signature, no provenance, no build record. Close the supply-chain gap.

steps.symptom: Production is running image api:2.7.3. No CI build produced that tag. Nobody knows what source it was built from.
evidence: api:2.7.3 deployed 2026-09-14 by manual kubectl apply.
CI built api:2.7.2 and api:2.7.4. No 2.7.3 anywhere.
options: Treat it as untrusted: quarantine, rebuild 2.7.3's claimed source in CI, and require signatures plus provenance before anything deploys
It's running fine — tag it as approved retroactively
Delete it immediately without investigation
Ask around until someone claims it
steps.explain: An untraceable artifact is an untrusted artifact. Sign what you build and attest where it came from (SLSA-style provenance); at deploy time, verification fails closed so tampering — or mystery builds — cannot promote.

steps.symptom: The team signs images now, but deploys a mutable 'latest' tag that CI overwrites.
evidence: Build pushes api:latest on every main commit. Deploy references api:latest.
'We deployed latest but got yesterday's code — the tag moved mid-deploy.'
options: Deploy immutable references — digests or version tags — so the manifest describes exactly what's running
Keep latest but deploy faster to beat the tag moves
Sign the latest tag more often
Ban tags entirely and use only digests typed by hand
steps.explain: Mutable tags make the deployment manifest a lie: 'latest' names a different artifact every hour. Immutable references (digest or pinned version) keep git honest about what's actually running — signatures then attest to that exact artifact.

steps.symptom: Signatures exist, but the deploy pipeline doesn't verify them — 'we trust our registry.'
evidence: No admission control. Any image reference deploys, signed or not.
Registry credentials are shared across 4 teams.
options: Enforce verification at deploy time with admission control — policy as code, not trust as policy
Trust is fine — the registry requires a login
Verify manually before important deploys
Shared registry credentials are the real problem — fix that instead
steps.explain: Policy as code makes requirements machine-enforced: an admission controller that rejects unsigned or unattested images turns the signature from a nice-to-have into a gate. 'We trust our registry' is wiki prose; the gate is enforcement.

simulations.debrief: Supply-chain integrity is signatures plus provenance, verified at deploy time, on immutable references. Each missing piece — the signature, the attestation, the verification, the immutability — is a gap attackers walk through.

simulations.title: Policy as suggestion
simulations.brief: The security wiki says 'all containers must run as non-root.' An audit of production finds 61% run as root. The policy has existed for two years. Make it real.

steps.symptom: Wiki policy: non-root containers. Reality: 61% of production containers run as root.
evidence: Production scan: 61% runAsUser 0. No enforcement mechanism exists anywhere.
options: Convert the prose to a machine-enforced gate: admission control that rejects root containers
Update the wiki with stronger language — 'MUST' in bold
Email the teams again about the policy
Accept 61% — the wiki was aspirational
steps.explain: Policy as code makes requirements machine-enforced gates rather than wiki prose. Two years of unenforced 'MUST' proves documentation doesn't change behavior — an admission controller that physically rejects non-compliant pods does.

steps.symptom: Three legacy services genuinely need root — they break under the new gate.
evidence: Services A, B, C: require root for legacy volume mounts. Migration planned Q2.
Admission controller now rejects all root containers cluster-wide. Deploys failing.
options: Grant scoped, expiring exceptions for the three services with a recorded sunset date — escape hatches with governance
Disable the gate — it breaks production
Rewrite the three services this weekend
Give every team a permanent root exemption
steps.explain: Gates need governed escape hatches: a scoped exception, a named owner, an expiry tied to the migration plan. That preserves the gate's integrity while acknowledging reality — unlike a global off-switch or permanent exemptions.

steps.symptom: A team asks: 'Can we get the same enforcement for image scanning and resource limits?'
evidence: 'The root gate worked. We want scan-clean and limits enforced the same way.'
Other unenforced wiki policies: 14 (scanning, limits, labels, network policies).
options: Expand policy-as-code to the next policies with the same pattern: gate, scoped exceptions, sunset dates
Say no — one gate is enough process
Enforce all 14 at once next Monday
Write a longer wiki page covering all 14
steps.explain: The pattern scales: each wiki-prose policy becomes a gate with governed exceptions. Roll them out incrementally — all 14 at once is a bigger blast radius than the organization can absorb, and another wiki page changes nothing.

simulations.debrief: Policy as code turns requirements into gates: non-compliant artifacts physically cannot promote. Pair every gate with governed, expiring exceptions — and expand the pattern instead of the wiki.

simulations.title: The SAST-only blind spot
simulations.brief: SAST runs on every PR and the dashboard is green. Then a runtime injection vulnerability ships to production — a class of bug SAST can't see. Layer the scanning.

steps.symptom: SAST green on every PR for a year. Production incident: runtime template injection via user input.
evidence: SAST: 0 findings on the vulnerable PR. Rule coverage: static patterns only.
Exploit: payload rendered server-side at runtime — no static signature existed for the sink.
options: Add DAST: runtime scanning sees behavior that static analysis can't — the layers cover each other's blind spots
SAST is broken — replace it with a different SAST tool
Ban templates — the feature is too dangerous
More SAST rules will eventually catch runtime issues
steps.explain: SAST, DAST, and SCA see different things: static flaws, runtime behavior, dependency vulnerabilities. A runtime injection is DAST's territory — no amount of static rules reliably catches what only manifests at execution.

steps.symptom: DAST is added but only runs nightly against staging — findings arrive days after the code merged.
evidence: Nightly run, staging only. Mean time from merge to finding: 3.2 days.
'By the time DAST reports, I've forgotten the code.'
options: Shift DAST left: run targeted runtime scans on PR environments so feedback lands while the code is still open
Nightly is fine — security takes time
Run DAST less often to reduce noise
Only scan production — that's where the risk is
steps.explain: Shift-left applies to every scan type: findings are cheapest where the code is still open in the author's mind. A 3-day feedback loop turns DAST into archaeology; PR-environment scans make it a conversation.

steps.symptom: Now SAST, DAST, and SCA all run — and developers drown in 200+ findings per PR.
evidence: Per PR: 200+ findings, 90% duplicates or unreachable. Developers bulk-dismiss.
The template-injection class: buried at position 147.
options: Tune and deduplicate: reachable-first ranking, baseline the legacy noise, gate only on new reachable findings
Turn off two scanners — one is enough
Findings are findings — developers must fix all 200
Hide the dashboard so developers aren't distracted
steps.explain: Layered scanning without tuning is a denial-of-service on developers. Deduplicate, rank by reachability, baseline legacy noise, and gate on what's new and reachable — the signal at position 147 is the one that matters.

simulations.debrief: Layer SAST, DAST, and SCA because each has blind spots the others cover — then tune the combined signal so developers see reachable findings first. Coverage without triage is just noise.

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
